name: Orthodontic functional appliances (Herbst, Twin Block)

lead: Functional appliances such as the Herbst and Twin Block hold the lower jaw forward in children and teens with a Class II bite, where the lower jaw sits behind the upper. The payoff is a better-balanced profile and bite while the face is still growing.

The Herbst uses telescoping rods fixed to the teeth; the Twin Block uses removable interlocking bite plates. The Twin Block was studied in a multicentre randomized trial in the United Kingdom in children aged 8 to 10. Research, including a systematic review, separates small amounts of extra lower-jaw growth and upper-jaw restraint from movement of the teeth themselves.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance, usually before or around the pubertal growth spurt. The Herbst is fixed, so it does not depend on remembering to wear it, and treatment typically runs for several months. The Twin Block is removable and worn as directed. Forum users ask about cost, adult use and cheaper substitutes.

Reported effects include initial discomfort, chewing and speech difficulty, spacing between teeth, and possible gum or root effects with heavy tooth movement. The appliances are designed for growing patients, and skeletal change in adults is limited without surgery. Over-the-counter substitutes have not been studied for this purpose.

web.title: Orthodontic functional appliances (Herbst, Twin Block) — Grokipedia

chain: Lower jaw grows or shifts forward
angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens, so the jaw grows or shifts forward and the profile and bite balance out. Randomized trials in adolescents have studied them, with debate over how much change is jaw growth versus tooth movement. Adult use for facial appearance is based on user reports.

lead: Orthodontic functional appliances are devices that hold or guide the lower jaw forward in growing children and adolescents, mainly to treat Class II malocclusion, in which the lower jaw sits behind the upper one and the upper front teeth overlap the lower ones. The best-known examples are the Herbst appliance, a fixed device with telescoping arms bonded to the teeth, and the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic bite plates [1][2].

The Herbst appliance was developed by the German orthodontist Emil Herbst in the early 1900s and reintroduced in modern form by Hans Pancherz in 1979 [1][3]. Because it is fixed, it does not depend on the patient remembering to wear it, and treatment typically runs for several months [1]. The Twin Block was studied in a multicentre randomized trial in the United Kingdom in children aged 8 to 10 [4].

Published research, including a systematic review, has examined how much of the correction comes from extra lower-jaw growth versus tooth movement [5][5]. Within looksmaxxing communities, the devices are discussed as a way to advance a 'recessed' jaw during the teenage years, and some users ask whether adults or home-made alternatives can achieve similar changes [6][7].
infobox: Fixed (Herbst) or removable (Twin Block) functional orthodontic appliance

paras: The Herbst appliance is anchored to teeth by bands or acrylic coverings and connects the upper and lower dental arches with telescoping rods on each side, so the lower jaw is held in a forward position while still allowing some opening [1]. It is typically attached to the upper molars and lower premolars and stays in place continuously [1]. Variants include spring-based versions such as the Sabbagh Spring, Powerscope and Cantilever Bite Jumper, and versions anchored to mini-screws rather than only to teeth [1][8].

The Twin Block consists of upper and lower removable acrylic plates with interlocking inclined bite blocks that guide the lower jaw forward when the patient closes [4]. Other removable functional appliances, such as the Fränkel FR-2 and the Bionator, work on similar principles [9].

Proponents of functional appliances propose that holding the lower jaw forward during growth stimulates remodelling at the jaw joint and additional growth of the mandible. Early cephalometric studies of the Herbst appliance in growing boys reported changes in occlusion and in jaw relationships over about six months, with contributions from both skeletal and dental changes [10][11]. Later imaging work followed the temporomandibular joint during Herbst treatment in adolescents and young adults [12].

Orthodontic literature distinguishes skeletal effects (changes in jaw size or position) from dentoalveolar effects (teeth tipping or moving within the bone), such as upper molars moving backward and lower front teeth tipping forward [1][5].

Orthodontists discuss timing relative to the pubertal growth spurt. Wikipedia reports that starting at or just after the pubertal peak has been associated with more stable results, while some studies found similar results before and after puberty [1]. A paper on Twin Block timing has also examined this question [13]. Clinical trials have compared prepubertal and postpubertal Herbst treatment [14].

A multicentre randomized controlled trial in the United Kingdom allocated 174 children aged 8 to 10 with Class II Division 1 malocclusion to a Twin Block or to no treatment and assessed dental and skeletal effects after 15 months [4]. A randomized trial also compared the Herbst appliance with the Twin Block [15]. A 2006 systematic review of randomized and controlled clinical studies examined whether functional appliances enhance mandibular growth in Class II patients [5].

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov have compared Herbst appliances with different anchorage types, with and without mini-implants, and against the Twin Block [16][17][18]. Other registered trials have examined effects before versus after puberty and effects on airway dimensions [14][19]. Evidence for outcomes in adults is limited; the Herbst appliance has also been tested as a mandibular advancement device in obstructive sleep apnea [20].

Wikipedia reports that unwanted spacing in the upper arch may occur and that patients can have initial discomfort or chewing difficulty during the first weeks [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, lists soft-tissue irritation, speech difficulty, root resorption and gum recession as potential issues with excessive tooth movement [2].

On looksmax.org, teenagers with a 'recessed' jaw or overbite ask about obtaining a Herbst appliance and whether it will affect the upper jaw [6][7]. One poster asked about alternatives and was pointed toward over-the-counter mouth guards; the original poster said they were skeptical of the product website [6]. Other threads ask whether Herbst, Twin Block or Bionator appliances affect the lower third of the face, or whether a Forsus appliance can be used without an obvious overbite [21][22]. One thread claims orthodontic treatment with Herbst appliances and elastics restrains upper-jaw growth [23]. Replies in one thread advise asking an orthodontist, noting that forum users are not professionals [7].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, functional appliances are discussed mainly by teenagers and parents weighing jaw-growth modification against later surgery, alongside questions about cost, access and substitutes [6][7][21].

claims.claim: A Herbst appliance can lengthen a short lower jaw and fix a 'recessed' look.
Herbst appliances and elastics stunt upper-jaw (maxillary) growth.
Cheap mouth guards or home-made devices can substitute for a Herbst.
Functional appliances can improve the lower third of the face in people who are no longer growing.

timeline.event: Emil Herbst develops the appliance and presents it in Berlin (dates vary between sources) [2].
Hans Pancherz reintroduces the Herbst appliance in a banded modern form and publishes a cephalometric study [3][1].
Studies compare the Twin Block and the Fränkel FR-2 with untreated controls [9].
Randomized trials of the Twin Block and of Herbst versus Twin Block are published [4][15].
A systematic review assesses mandibular changes with functional appliances [5].
